fixes.explanation: I see why this one came to mind. Obed-edom, a man whose household once kept the ark in his house, had it for three months (1 Chronicles 13:14). But that's not what David says here. He tells Nathan the prophet it's under a tent, while he sits in a house of cedar.

Shiloh never comes up in this passage. David, Israel's king, says the ark of the covenant of the LORD is under a tent. He says it while he's living in a house of cedar. Nathan the prophet is the one listening.

That's what God tells Nathan to say: "You are not the one to build Me a house in which to dwell." God calls David "My servant" in the same breath. Nathan told David, "Do all that is in your heart," and that night the word of God came to him. A prophet has to be ready to update his answer.

The text says the opposite. God asks, "In all My journeys with all the Israelites, have I ever asked any of the leaders I appointed to shepherd My people, ‘Why haven’t you built Me a house of cedar?’" The question points to no, because He had never asked any of them. Not one leader was ever asked.

God puts it as a question: "In all My journeys with all the Israelites, have I ever asked any of the leaders I appointed to shepherd My people, ‘Why haven’t you built Me a house of cedar?’" The question points to no. In all those journeys, He never asked any of them. Not one of them was ever asked.

God says, "I took you from the pasture, from following the flock, to be the ruler over My people Israel." David's start was following the flock. God points back to it as part of how far he's come. I think that's a gentle reminder of who put him where he is.

The text doesn't say army here. God says, "I took you from the pasture, from following the flock, to be the ruler over My people Israel." So David's starting point was the pasture, not a battlefield. He went from following a flock to ruling.
No plow in this verse. God says, "I took you from the pasture, from following the flock…" So David was following a flock, not farming a field. A flock, not a field.

The text says the opposite. God says He will plant His people so they may dwell in a place of their own and be disturbed no more. Then He says, "No longer will the sons of wickedness oppress them as they did at the beginning…" So the sons of wickedness won't oppress them like that anymore once they're planted.

God promises a place of their own where they will be "…disturbed no more." Then He says, "No longer will the sons of wickedness oppress them as they did at the beginning…" So they won't be oppressed like that anymore once they're planted. That's a promise worth sitting down for.

David wanted to build God a house, and God flips it around. He says, "Moreover, I declare to you that the LORD will build a house for you." I think David didn't see that coming. He wanted to build God a house, and God answered with a promise to build his.
A water tunnel? Not in this promise, friend. About David's son, God says, "He will build a house for Me…" That's the one job on the table, and I'd say it's a big enough job already.
God says, "…I will establish his throne forever." He says it again a couple of verses later: "…his throne will be established forever." That's no short-term promise.
David doesn't ask that. His first words to the LORD are, "Who am I, O LORD God, and what is my house, that You have brought me this far?" He opens with who he is, not with a schedule.

Tests? Not the word here. David says, "What more can David say to You for honoring Your servant? For You know Your servant…" He's talking about being honored and known, and I think that's a much warmer word than tests.
Time? Friend, David's calendar isn't the issue. He says, "Therefore Your servant has found the courage to pray before You." God's revelation is what gave him that courage.
